title: How to Slice Sweet Potatoes for Crispy Fries Using a Mandoline
meta_description: Master the art of making crispy fries. Learn to slice sweet potatoes mandoline style for even results and perfect crunch every time.
html:
There is nothing more disappointing than pulling a tray of sweet potato fries out of the oven only to find that half are burnt while the others are still raw in the middle. The culprit is almost always inconsistent thickness. To get that restaurant-quality crunch at home, you need to learn how to slice sweet potatoes mandoline style. This tool takes the guesswork out of prep work, ensuring every fry cooks at the exact same speed for perfect texture.

Why Precision Matters for Sweet Potatoes

Sweet potatoes are structurally different from russets. They have a higher sugar content and a denser, more fibrous flesh. Because of this density, a thick-cut fry will take significantly longer to cook through than a thin one. If you try to hand-cut them with a knife, you inevitably end up with wedges that vary in size.

The solution is a Mandoline Slicer. This gadget provides restaurant-thin, even slices of veggies and fruit fast—adjustable mandolines with hand guards allow you to dial in the exact thickness you need. When every fry is exactly 1/4-inch thick, they all caramelize evenly in the oven without leaving you with soggy bottoms or burnt tips.

Prep Work: Getting the Potato Ready

Before you even touch the blade, you need to stabilize the potato. Sweet potatoes can be notoriously knobby and irregular, which is a safety hazard on a slicer. Start by peeling the potato completely. While you can leave the skin on for texture, removing it ensures a uniform cook and prevents the skin from tearing unevenly as it passes over the blade.

Next, you need to create a flat surface. Take a sharp chef’s knife and cut a thin slice off one side of the potato lengthwise. Lay the potato on this newly cut flat side. It should sit steady on the cutting board without rocking. If the potato is very long, you can cut it in half crosswise to make it easier to manage.

How to Slice Sweet Potatoes Mandoline Style

Now that your potato is prepped, it is time to use the tool. Do not rely on speed; rely on technique. Here is the safest and most effective method to get those perfect sticks:

  1. Set your thickness. For standard fries, set your Mandoline Slicer to the 1/4-inch setting. If you prefer shoestring fries, go thinner, but remember that thinner fries burn faster.
  2. Secure the guard. Place the potato flat side down onto the hand guard’s spikes. Ensure it is pierced deeply so it doesn't slip while you apply pressure.
  3. The slicing motion. Hold the handle of the mandoline firmly with one hand. With the other, slide the guard (containing the potato) down the ramp in a smooth, continuous motion. Do not stop halfway through.
  4. Protect your fingers. As the potato gets smaller, you will be tempted to remove the guard and use your fingers. Don't do it. Use the small piece of potato provided with the guard or a specialized safety pusher to slice the remaining bits. No fry is worth a cut fingertip.

From Mandoline to Oven: Cooking for Crispiness

Once you have your evenly sliced potatoes, the cooking process is straightforward, but there is one secret step: soaking. Because you used a mandoline to create perfect surfaces, the potatoes have a lot of exposed starch. Rinse the slices in cold water until the water runs clear, then soak them for 30 minutes.

After soaking, dry them—really dry them. Use a clean kitchen towel or paper towels to pat them completely dry. Excess moisture is the enemy of crispiness. Toss them with a light coating of oil (avocado or peanut oil works best due to their high smoke points), salt, and your favorite spices. Spread them on a baking sheet in a single layer; if they are touching, they will steam instead of bake.

Safety Tips You Can't Ignore

It bears repeating: mandolines are incredibly sharp. They are designed to cut through hard vegetables with minimal effort, which means they can slice through skin instantly. Always use the hand guard that comes with the Mandoline Slicer. If your model comes with cut-resistant gloves, wear them. Keep your eye on the blade, not the potato, and keep the tool away from the edge of the counter where it might be knocked off. When cleaning the mandoline, do not run your hand over the blade; use a brush or the designated cleaning tool if your kit includes one.

FAQ

Do I have to peel the sweet potato before using the mandoline?

While you can leave the skin on if you prefer a rustic texture, peeling them is highly recommended. The skin can be tough and catch on the blade, causing the potato to slip or the slice to tear unevenly. Peeling ensures the smoothest possible slice for even cooking.

Why are my fries still soggy even after slicing them evenly?

If you used your Mandoline Slicer to get the thickness right but still ended up with soggy fries, you likely skipped the drying step. After rinsing the starch off, the potatoes must be patted completely dry with a towel before hitting the hot oil or oven. Moisture creates steam; heat creates crunch.

Can I use a mandoline for baked sweet potato chips too?

Absolutely. In fact, a mandoline is the only way to get chips thin enough to crisp up properly. Just switch the setting to the thinnest option (usually 1/8-inch or less). Keep a close eye on them in the oven, however, because paper-thin slices can go from perfect to burnt in a matter of seconds.
